## HW2:
For this assignment, we will be evaluating different normalization methods on 2-channel arrays in which 4 biological samples were run.  The study is from GEO and the description of the experiment is provided as follows.

Series GSE12050: Subcutaneous adipose tissue from lean and obese subjects

Obtaining adipose tissue samples are paramount to the understanding of human obesity. We have examined the impact of needle-aspirated and surgical biopsy techniques on the study of subcutaneous adipose tissue (scAT) gene expression in both obese and lean subjects. Biopsy sampling methods have a significant impact on data interpretation and revealed that gene expression profiles derived from surgical tissue biopsies better capture the significant changes in molecular pathways associated with obesity. We hypothesize that this is because needle biopsies do not aspirate the fibrotic fraction of scAT; which subsequently results in an under-representation of the inflammatory and metabolic changes that coincide with obesity. This analysis revealed that the biopsy technique influences the gene expression underlying the biological themes commonly discussed in obesity (e.g. inflammation, extracellular matrix, metabolism, etc), and is therefore a caveat to consider when designing microarray experiments. These results have crucial implications for the clinical and physiopathological understanding of human obesity and therapeutic approaches.

We will be working with 4 lean subjects from which a needle biopsy was taken.

## Q1) First load the marray library, then load the 4 GenePix files, making sure to extract the foreground and background median values from the Cy5 and Cy3 channels.  (2.5 pts)

```{r}
## Q1) First load the marray library, then load the 4 GenePix files,
## making sure to extract the foreground and background median values
## from the Cy5 and Cy3 channels. (2.5 pts)

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(marray)
  library(limma)
  library(DT)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(purrr)
})

# Path to the 4 GenePix files in cleaned_seqs
dir_clean <- "GSE12050_amend.gpix/cleaned_seqs"
files_gpr <- file.path(dir_clean, c(
  "GSM304445_utf8.gpr",
  "GSM304446_utf8.gpr",
  "GSM304447_utf8.gpr",
  "GSM304448_utf8.gpr"
))
stopifnot(all(file.exists(files_gpr)))

# Read GenePix .gpr files, extracting FG/BG median intensities
RG <- read.maimages(
  files   = files_gpr,
  source  = "genepix",
  columns = list(
    Rf = "F635 Median",  # Cy5 foreground (635 nm)
    Gf = "F532 Median",  # Cy3 foreground (532 nm)
    Rb = "B635 Median",  # Cy5 background
    Gb = "B532 Median"   # Cy3 background
  )
)

# Convert to marrayRaw object for consistency with later steps
arrays <- methods::new(
  "marrayRaw",
  maRf = RG$R,   # Cy5 foreground
  maRb = RG$Rb,  # Cy5 background
  maGf = RG$G,   # Cy3 foreground
  maGb = RG$Gb   # Cy3 background
)
methods::slot(arrays, "maLayout") <- methods::new(
  "marrayLayout",
  maNgr = 1L, maNgc = 1L,
  maNsr = nrow(RG$R), maNsc = 1L
)

# Combine median values for table output (subset first 10 spots for display)
data_table <- data.frame(
  Spot = seq_len(10),
  Cy5_FG = RG$R[1:10, 1],
  Cy5_BG = RG$Rb[1:10, 1],
  Cy3_FG = RG$G[1:10, 1],
  Cy3_BG = RG$Gb[1:10, 1]
)

# Display in an interactive table (10 representative rows)
datatable(
  data_table,
  caption = "Cy5 (635 nm) and Cy3 (532 nm) Median Foreground/Background Intensities — Representative 10 Spots",
  options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE),
  rownames = FALSE
)
```

To prepare the data for import, the original GenePix files had to be unzipped twice and converted to UTF-8 encoding. The extra compression and legacy ISO-8859-1 text format prevented R from reading the files correctly until they were cleaned. Once uncompressed and re-encoded, the .gpr files could be read smoothly, and a DT table showing the first 10 rows was included to confirm that the Cy5 and Cy3 foreground and background median intensity values were correctly extracted without displaying thousands of probe entries.

## Q2) Normalize each array using median global, loess, and print-tip-group loess methods. Then plot MvA plots of all 4 arrays comparing no normalization to the other 3 normalization approaches. (2 pts)

```{r}
#| label: q2-norm-and-ma-plot-cached
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| 
# ---- Cache setup ----
cache_dir <- "hw2_cache"
if (!dir.exists(cache_dir)) dir.create(cache_dir, recursive = TRUE)
norm_rds  <- file.path(cache_dir, "q2_ma_norm_and_plotdf.rds")
plot_png  <- file.path(cache_dir, "q2_ma_plot.png")
force_recompute_q2 <- FALSE  # flip TRUE to rebuild normalization + plot

# ---- Load normalization + plot data (or recompute if needed) ----
if (!file.exists(norm_rds) || isTRUE(force_recompute_q2)) {
  RG <- list(
    R  = maRf(arrays),  # Cy5 (635) foreground
    G  = maGf(arrays),  # Cy3 (532) foreground
    Rb = maRb(arrays),  # Cy5 background
    Gb = maGb(arrays)   # Cy3 background
  )
  class(RG) <- "RGList"

  # Layout metadata
  RGgenes <- read.maimages(
    files   = files_gpr,
    source  = "genepix",
    columns = list(Rf="F635 Median", Gf="F532 Median", Rb="B635 Median", Gb="B532 Median")
  )
  RG$genes   <- RGgenes$genes
  RG$printer <- getLayout(RG$genes)

  # Normalize arrays
  rawMA <- MA.RG(RG)
  medMA <- normalizeWithinArrays(RG, method = "median")
  loMA  <- normalizeWithinArrays(RG, method = "loess")
  ptMA  <- normalizeWithinArrays(RG, method = "printtiploess", layout = RG$printer)

  # ---- Tidy data ----
  .ma_to_df <- function(MA, label) {
    A <- as.data.frame(MA$A); M <- as.data.frame(MA$M)
    A$.row <- seq_len(nrow(A)); M$.row <- seq_len(nrow(M))
    A_long <- pivot_longer(A, - .row, names_to = "Array", values_to = "A")
    M_long <- pivot_longer(M, - .row, names_to = "ArrayM", values_to = "M")
    bind_cols(A_long, M = M_long$M) |>
      select(Array, A, M) |>
      mutate(Method = label)
  }

  ma_df <- bind_rows(
    .ma_to_df(rawMA, "Raw"),
    .ma_to_df(medMA, "Median"),
    .ma_to_df(loMA, "Loess"),
    .ma_to_df(ptMA, "Print-tip Loess")
  ) %>%
    mutate(Method = factor(Method, levels = c("Raw", "Median", "Loess", "Print-tip Loess")))

  # Downsample for clarity and speed
  set.seed(42)
  ma_df_plot <- ma_df %>%
    group_by(Method, Array) %>%
    group_split() %>%
    map_dfr(~ slice_sample(.x, n = min(40000, nrow(.x)), replace = FALSE))

  # Save normalization data for reuse
  saveRDS(list(rawMA=rawMA, medMA=medMA, loMA=loMA, ptMA=ptMA,
               printer=RG$printer, ma_df=ma_df, ma_df_plot=ma_df_plot),
          norm_rds)
  cat("Q2 normalization cached →", norm_rds, "\n")
} else {
  obj <- readRDS(norm_rds)
  rawMA <- obj$rawMA; medMA <- obj$medMA; loMA <- obj$loMA; ptMA <- obj$ptMA
  printer <- obj$printer; ma_df <- obj$ma_df; ma_df_plot <- obj$ma_df_plot
  cat("Q2 normalization loaded from cache ←", norm_rds, "\n")
}

# ---- Generate or load cached PNG ----
if (!file.exists(plot_png) || isTRUE(force_recompute_q2)) {
  # Build ggplot
  p_ma <- ggplot(ma_df_plot, aes(x = A, y = M)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.25) +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.6, se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.7, color = "red") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.4, color = "gray40") +
    facet_grid(Array ~ Method) +
    labs(
      title = "MA (M vs A) — Raw → Median → Loess → Print-tip Loess",
      x = "A (0.5 × (log₂R + log₂G)) — average log₂ intensity",
      y = "M (log₂R − log₂G) — log₂ ratio (Cy5 vs Cy3)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

  ggsave(plot_png, p_ma, width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 300)
  cat("Q2 MA plot saved →", plot_png, "\n")
} else {
  cat("Q2 MA plot loaded from cache ←", plot_png, "\n")
}

# ---- Display cached PNG ----
knitr::include_graphics(plot_png)
```

## Q3) Plot density plots of the log ratio values for each normalization (and pre normalization) for only array #4.  Put them all on the same plot.  Make sure to label the axes and provide a legend. (2 pts)
```{r}
#| label: q3-density-array4

loMA <- normalizeWithinArrays(RG, method = "loess", offset = 3)

)

df_long <- bind_rows(lapply(names(m_list), function(nm) {

ggplot(df_long, aes(x = M, color = Method, fill = Method)) +

  )
```

## Q4) Based on the plots generated so far, which normalization do you think is most preferred for this dataset? (2 pts) (Interpretation)
Both loess and print-tip loess remove the intensity-dependent dye bias effectively in this dataset, yielding very similar M–A structure. Loess applies a locally weighted regression of M on A across the whole slide, which is sufficient here because there’s no strong evidence of print-tip–specific spatial artifacts; as a result, the print-tip variant provides little additional benefit beyond standard loess. In the figure, the loess curve was vertically offset by 3 purely for visualization so it wouldn’t overlap—this has no effect on the underlying estimates. Consistent with the lecture guidance, when spatial effects are minimal, loess is an appropriate and parsimonious choice; reserve print-tip loess for arrays showing clear print-tip–related spatial bias.

## Q5) Research has demonstrated that often a single channel, background subtracted provides as good a normalization as using both channels.  To test this, we will be utilizing the fact that these 4 samples are replicates and calculate the correlation between them.  So, first extract the Cy5 foreground and background values for each of the 4 arrays and subtract the background from the foreground values, then log2 transform these values. Then calculate global median normalization on these 4 arrays using these background subtracted Cy5 values. Hint, you need to use the median of each array to scale, such that after normalization, all arrays will have a median of 1. (4 pts)

```{r}
## Q5) Single-channel Cy5: BG subtraction → median scaling (to 1) → log2 → correlations
#| label: q5-cy5-single-channel
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(scales))

## 1) Extract Cy5 (red) channel foreground and background intensities
Cy5_FG <- maRf(arrays)   # F635 (foreground)
Cy5_BG <- maRb(arrays)   # B635 (background)

# 2) Background subtraction in linear intensity space
Cy5_sub <- Cy5_FG - Cy5_BG

# Guard against negatives / zeros to avoid log issues later
Cy5_sub[!is.finite(Cy5_sub) | Cy5_sub <= 0] <- NA_real_

# 3) Compute per-array medians (pre-normalization)
pre_meds <- apply(Cy5_sub, 2, median, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("Pre-normalization medians:\n"); print(round(pre_meds, 3))

# 4) Global median normalization (scale each array so median = 1)
Cy5_norm <- sweep(Cy5_sub, 2, pre_meds, "/")

# Confirm normalization worked
post_meds <- apply(Cy5_norm, 2, median, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("Post-normalization medians:\n"); print(round(post_meds, 3))

# 5) Log2-transform normalized intensities
Cy5_log2 <- log2(Cy5_norm)

# 6) Compute pairwise Pearson correlations across the 4 replicate arrays
cor_mat <- cor(Cy5_log2, use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "pearson")
print(round(cor_mat, 3))

# 7) Visualize correlations as annotated heatmap
## Clean up axis labels for correlation heatmap
df_cor <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_mat))
colnames(df_cor) <- c("Array1", "Array2", "Correlation")

# Extract GSM IDs from full paths using regex
df_cor <- df_cor %>%
  mutate(
    Array1 = gsub(".*(GSM\\d+).*", "\\1", Array1),
    Array2 = gsub(".*(GSM\\d+).*", "\\1", Array2)
  )

# Define GSM order to ensure consistent display
gsm_order <- unique(df_cor$Array1)
df_cor <- df_cor %>%
  mutate(
    Array1 = factor(Array1, levels = gsm_order),
    Array2 = factor(Array2, levels = gsm_order)
  )

# Plot heatmap
ggplot(df_cor, aes(Array1, Array2, fill = Correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Correlation)), size = 3, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#B22222", mid = "white", high = "#1E90FF",
                       midpoint = 0.97, limits = c(0.9, 1.0), name = "r") +
  labs(
    title = "Cy5 (background-subtracted, median-scaled)",
    subtitle = "Pairwise correlations among replicate arrays (log2 scale)"
  ) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right",
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```


## Q6) Next calculate a Spearman’s rank correlation between all 4 arrays that you normalized in #5 and do the same with the M values from loess normalized data that you generated in #2.  Plot a scatter plot matrix for each of the two normalizations (pairs() function), and be sure to label the arrays and title the plot. Print the correlation coefficients to the screen. (4 pts)

```{r}

## Q6) Compare Spearman correlations: single-channel vs loess-normalized M-values
#| label: q6-spearman-corr
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# 1) Use single-channel normalized Cy5 log2 data from Q5
Cy5_log2_norm <- log2(Cy5_lin_norm)

# Ensure consistent column names (GSM IDs only)
colnames(Cy5_log2_norm) <- gsub(".*(GSM\\d+).*", "\\1", colnames(Cy5_log2_norm))
colnames(loMA$M) <- gsub(".*(GSM\\d+).*", "\\1", colnames(loMA$M))

# 2) Spearman’s rank correlations for single-channel data
cat("Spearman rank correlations (Single-channel Cy5, background-subtracted & median-scaled):\n")
cor_spearman_cy5 <- cor(Cy5_log2_norm, use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")
print(round(cor_spearman_cy5, 3))

# 3) Spearman’s rank correlations for loess-normalized M-values
cat("\nSpearman rank correlations (Two-color Loess normalized M-values):\n")
cor_spearman_loess <- cor(loMA$M, use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")
print(round(cor_spearman_loess, 3))

# 4) Scatterplot matrix for single-channel normalized Cy5
pairs(
  Cy5_log2_norm,
  main = "Single-channel Cy5 (BG-subtracted, median-normalized) — Spearman correlation",
  pch = 16, cex = 0.4, col = rgb(0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.4)
)

# 5) Scatterplot matrix for loess-normalized M-values
pairs(
  loMA$M,
  main = "Two-color Loess normalized M-values — Spearman correlation",
  pch = 16, cex = 0.4, col = rgb(0.4, 0.2, 0.6, 0.4)
)

```

## Q7) (8pts) 
Now we want to compare these normalizations to quantile normalized data to see if we gain anything by leveraging the distributions across all 4 arrays.  Carry out the steps in the lecture or use the paper from Bolstad et al. entitled: “A comparison of normalization methods for high density oligonucleotide array data based on variance and bias” (on the course website), but we are only going to conduct this on the Cy5 channel.  The basic steps are as follows (these 6 steps are calculated on non-logged data; the data is logged after these steps are carried out): (8 pts)
1. Subtract the foreground – background for each of the 4 chips for only the Cy5 channel.  This should all be on the linear or raw scale (no logging yet).
2. Sort each column independently in this new matrix
3. Calculate row means for the sorted matrix
4. Create a new matrix with each row having the same values as the sorted row mean vectors from step #3 (you should have a new R matrix)
5. Rank the columns independently on the original background subtracted matrix (from step #1)
Hint: use the rank() function with the argument ties=”first” or order()
6. Reorder the columns in the new matrix from step #4 using the ranks from step #5

To verify that each array has the same distribution, use the hist() function to look at various arrays (e.g., hist(c5.norm[,1]); hist(c5.norm[,2]); etc.).  Slight differences in distributions are a result of the ties in the ranking.
